metadata.title: The dietary fibre content of fruit and vegetable kitchen preparation waste and UK consumers’ dietary fibre-related attitudes regarding its consumption

paper_text_source: bundle:issue-106 (supplied PDF, emailed, staged in the papers repository and normalised by scripts/paper_bundle.py)
verification_changes: Theo cited episode ninety-three as fibre coming mostly from grains; card 93 says the protective fibre signal was from ultra-processed sources, with whole-grain fibre only the authors' interpretation

Theo said hosts should hide root-to-tip in normal food and takeaway three and the show notes said people want it hidden; participants also asked for the health benefits to be advertised, and the paper says only 'as natural as possible'
The kale insoluble-to-soluble ratio (slightly more insoluble) comes from the row whose fractions do not sum to its total; replaced with beetroot's under two to one (Table 3)
Nadia stated broccoli stalk is wetter as fact; the authors suggest moisture citing Campas-Baypoli et al., not their own measurement
Nadia said the literature table answers how much one specimen differs from the next; the table mixes AOAC, crude and neutral detergent fibre, so it only hints; dropped the derived threefold
Nadia said the paper used the method recommendations are built on, which the paper never states; now the authors' argument that total fibre is the relevant measure for consumers
Theo said episode ninety-one's men 'nobody' described pleasure; card 91 says they rarely did
'Tissues are structural and protective' is the authors' interpretation; attributed to them
The flesh values came from the GB23 database in Nutritics; dropped the unsupported 'national'
Cut kiwi's 'close to eight' from a turn already carrying two figures
Turns 26-27 were both Nadia, with 27 answering a question nobody asked, and turns 62-63 were both Theo; merged each pair

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Hi, and welcome to Science TLDR. I'm Nadia.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I'm Theo. And I'm told today involves eating the bits of the vegetable that usually go in the bin.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It does. In the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, Browne and colleagues at King's College London: "The dietary fibre content of fruit and vegetable kitchen preparation waste and U-K consumers' dietary fibre-related attitudes regarding its consumption." The short version: they measured the fibre in peels, stalks, cores and seeds of twelve kinds of produce, and ran focus groups on whether people would eat them.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So why is that worth ten minutes? Eat your broccoli stalks is advice my grandmother gave for free.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Because your grandmother never had a number for it, and neither did the reference databases. The U-K composition tables mostly don't list these parts, on the assumption nobody eats them, and where the literature has values, they were measured for industry and reported per dry weight.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Which is the wrong unit for someone holding a raw pineapple skin. It's mostly water.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Exactly. And it matters because fibre intake in the U-K is low: the authors cite national data that only about four percent of adults reach the thirty gram a day recommendation.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Four percent. So nearly everyone misses it.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Nearly everyone; the average is around sixteen grams. Meanwhile fresh produce is a big slice of food waste. Root-to-tip eating, the term of art, means cooking with the parts normally discarded, and promises to chip at both.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. What did they actually do?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Two studies in one paper. First, chemistry. The university's catering team picked twelve items that could go on a menu, from beetroot and kale to kiwi and pineapple. A professional chef prepared one of each, and the trimmings were weighed, freeze-dried and analysed.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: One of each. One butternut squash.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: One butternut squash. I'll come back to that. The assay is the standard enzymatic-gravimetric method: digest away the starch and protein, and what survives, corrected for protein and ash, is fibre. It splits into insoluble fibre, the cellulose-type scaffold, and soluble fibre, like some pectins.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So the claim is?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The central claim is that the discarded parts are richer in fibre than the parts we normally eat, in ten of the twelve, and so cooking with them is a viable way to raise intake.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Ten of twelve. How big are the numbers?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: The discarded parts ran from about two grams of fibre per hundred grams, watermelon rind, up to about nine and a quarter, butternut squash skin and seeds.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the flesh, for comparison?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Pineapple is the extreme. The skin and core came in at about six and a half grams, against about one point two for the flesh.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Oh, so that's more than five times as much.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's the four hundred and fifty percent in the paper. Watermelon is similar in proportion, but the flesh has almost none, so the rind wins while still being the lowest value in the set.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Hmm. A big percentage off a tiny denominator.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yes, though the absolute numbers are in the table. The two that went the other way were broccoli and fennel: broccoli stalk had less fibre than the florets, by more than a quarter. The authors suggest moisture, citing another study where the stalk was wetter, so per fresh gram there's less of everything.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That's a nice honest result to report, actually. It cuts against the folk wisdom.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And how much of the vegetable are we talking about? The trimmings were between a quarter and nearly half of each item by weight, leek at the top. So it's not a garnish; it's a real fraction of what you buy.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Though even the richest one is under ten grams of fibre per hundred. When the average intake is barely more than half the target, that's helpful, not a fix.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Agreed. And credit where due: for celeriac skin, kale stalk and fennel core, they found no published values at all, so those rows are new. The other consistent pattern is the type of fibre: in every one, insoluble outweighed soluble, from under two to one in beetroot to more than eight to one in watermelon rind. The authors read that as fitting what these tissues are for: peels and stalks are structural and protective.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay, now the reviewer question. Ten of twelve higher than what? Who measured the flesh?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Uh, nobody, in this study. The discarded parts were measured in their lab. The eaten parts weren't measured at all; their values come from a food composition database.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Wait. So it's one specimen of one squash, measured in-house, against a database average for squash flesh.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's right. Different specimens, different lab. The database isn't bad; the comparison just isn't paired.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the clean version was sitting on the chopping board. The flesh of the same squash, same assay, same day. Another dozen samples.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: And it matters most where the gap is small. Curly kale stalk beat the leaf by under seven percent. With one specimen and an unpaired reference, I'd call that a tie.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So the honest count is more like nine clear wins, one tie, two losses.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: I think that's fair for kale. The big ones, pineapple, squash, kiwi, pepper, are large enough that I doubt the pairing would flip them. The direction there I believe.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And the duplicates they report?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Um, those are two measurements of the same dried powder. Repeatable assay; nothing about how one squash differs from the next. The authors say themselves that multiple samples would strengthen the study.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: How much can one squash differ from the next?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Their own literature table hints at it, though it mixes methods. Published values for pineapple peel, per dry weight, run from the mid-twenties to over eighty grams per hundred.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Huh. So the literature is all over the place.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Partly variety and growing conditions, partly method. Some studies used crude fibre, which destroys most of the non-cellulose fibre; others neutral detergent fibre, which loses the soluble part. The authors are careful to say these aren't measuring the same thing.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: This is the instrument problem again. In episode ninety-one, the young men's consent interviews, the guide never asked about pleasure, so of course few described it. Here, pick crude fibre and you get a low number before you've touched a vegetable.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Yeah, same lesson, different bench. And it's a point in this paper's favour: they used the standard total-fibre method, which the authors argue is the relevant one for what people actually eat.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: There was something odd in one of the tables, though, wasn't there?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: There is. Total fibre is supposed to be the sum of the insoluble and soluble fractions, and for most rows it is. For curly kale the fractions add up to over ten grams, against a total of about four. Something in that row is wrong, and the table can't tell you what.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: And I noticed the literature table gives a second set of totals for the same samples, which don't match the main table. Pineapple drops about a gram.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Right, and the paper doesn't explain it. None of it reverses the headline, but a reader shouldn't have to reconcile it.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay. Energy. You said they measured that too.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: By bomb calorimetry, which burns the sample completely, fibre included. The trimmings came out higher than the flesh in eight of twelve.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Against database flesh values again, which are meant to be energy you can actually use. A calorimeter counts the fibre you can't digest. I wouldn't read much into that comparison.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Nor would I. The authors themselves argue that energy locked in intact plant cells isn't all absorbed.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Right. Let's do the people part. The focus groups.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Six groups, forty participants, staff and students who eat at the university's outlets, recruited by convenience and paid a voucher. Three quarters were women, many with postgraduate degrees. One researcher coded the transcripts.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Forty is reasonable for focus groups. We had five undergraduates in an A-D-H-D study once and that was thin.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Forty is fine for finding the range of views, not their frequency. The headline is that nutrition persuaded more than sustainability. Taste, price and health drove most people's purchases often or always; in the chart, not one person said sustainability always did.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Not one. On a university campus, which I'd have guessed was the friendliest audience for that pitch.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Mm-hm. The most useful finding is a quote. Someone said they wouldn't pick a dish because it advertised peels and stalks, but if they ate what they normally ate and were told it had two grams more fibre, they'd think, oh great, I feel healthy.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: That's a design spec, really. Make it normal food first, and mention the fibre after.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Which the authors take on board: participants did want the health benefits advertised, from reputable sources, but root-to-tip should feel as natural as possible.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Do I worry about the setup, though? Did the participants know what the study was for?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Well... yes. The paper says participants knew the study's aims. So the room that said fibre was a good selling point for peels knew that was the hypothesis.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Plus one coder, no pilot of the guide, an educated campus sample, which the authors flag. And it was registered a few months after the last focus group. I'd treat the themes as a starting list for a menu trial, not a finding about U-K consumers. What's not in here at all?

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Three things the authors name. Everything was raw, and cooking changes fibre. Safety: peels can carry more pesticide residue, and pineapple skin has cyanogenic compounds. And whether people given a root-to-tip menu eat more fibre and waste less. That trial exists; its results aren't here.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: So the conclusion that this is a viable strategy is really a prediction.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: It's a plausibility argument. They've shown the fibre is there. Not that it gets eaten, not that it's tolerated, not what it does once eaten.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: On what it does, episode ninety-three is the fair context. In that colorectal cancer cohort, fibre looked protective only when it came from ultra-processed sources, which the authors read as whole-grain fibre, and it was measured by questionnaire. Peel fibre is mostly insoluble, and the authors note fibre type changes how it behaves in the gut.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Right, and they don't claim health benefits from their own data.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Okay, my three takeaways. One: in most of these twelve items, the trimmings carry more fibre per gram than the part we eat, sometimes several times more, and it's mostly insoluble fibre. Broccoli stalk and fennel go the other way.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Two: that comparison is one specimen measured in-house against database values for the flesh. Big gaps like pineapple probably survive; small ones like kale don't count, and the kale row has an arithmetic problem.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Three: the focus groups suggest health beats sustainability as a pitch, and that the dishes should feel like normal food, but they come from a campus sample that knew the hypothesis.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: What would change my mind: paired measurements, several specimens of each, raw and cooked. If the pineapple and squash gaps hold up across five or six of each, that's a useful table for every dietitian.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: For me it's the menu trial. Show me the fibre actually eaten and the plate waste, not the fibre on the chopping board.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: That's the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, Browne and colleagues, D-O-I ten dot one zero eight zero slash zero nine six three seven four eight six dot two zero two six dot two seven three four eight five two.

turns.speaker: Theo
turns.text: Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: Nadia
turns.text: Take care, and see you next time.
